rendered:
The paper gives no amount of nickel, manganese or cobalt leaching into Cyrene. It states the opposite: the process does not leach those transition metals[1]. The basis is that the relative ratios of Ni, Mn and Co in the NMC622 were consistent before and after separation, as the paper puts it: the relative ratios of Ni, Mn, and Co from[2] NMC622 were consistent before and after the separation process[3]. The paper says this was also confirmed by ICP-OES results, shown in Table S1[4], which is a supplementary table not included in this document.

The leaching the paper does report is lithium: lithium leaching from NMC622[5] curred after recovery.[6]

The ether groups are blamed for this. In the paper's words: The Cyrene molecule has two ether groups,[7] which will attract lithium cation because ether is electron-donating,[8] resulting in lithium leaching and causing the high-Ni cathode more[9] unstable.[10]

So, according to the paper, the electron-donating ether groups pull lithium out of the cathode, which makes the high-Ni cathode less stable. Later the paper ties the electrochemical degradation to this lithium loss and to possible surface changes from the solvent: tributed to both the lithium leaching and possible surface changes[11].

The only Ni, Mn and Co values in the paper are EDX readings in the figure panels, which are surface mass percentages and are not presented as dissolved amounts. The figure text lists Ni 28.59[12] among its EDX values: Fig. 3[13]
